items.title: The void marriage and the invisible widow: Why the law needs an equitable answer
items.summary: A woman can spend her adult life with a man, raise his children, run his household and give up her career, and still walk away with nothing the day he dies, because a court later finds the marriage void. This recurs whenever a marriage falls foul of Section 5, read with Section 11, of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (HMA). The woman never becomes a wife in the eyes of law, so she can never become a widow either. And the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (HSA) has no room for her. The answer is not to pretend the marriage was valid. It lies in something the HMA already accepts: that the legal fate of a relationship and its economic consequences need not be tied together. Section 16 legitimises children of void and voidable marriages without validating the marriage. The same idea can be extended, carefully and narrowly, to the woman who lived the marriage in good faith. The statutory bind Section 5(i) requires that neither party have a living spouse at the time of marriage. Section 11 declares a marriage in breach void from inception (Section 12 covers voidable marriages), so the woman never becomes a wife. What happens when journalists covering protests are detained by the police, and what does it mean for press freedom and the right to dissent in India? In this week’s South Central, hosts Dhanya Rajendran and Anisha Sheth examine the crackdown’s implications for independent media, press freedom and the right to protest. They are joined by Siddharth Varadarajan, founding editor of The Wire , and Abhinandan Sekhri of Newslaundry , to discuss allegations of police violence, the targeting of journalists documenting the protests, and the lack of a stronger collective response from mainstream media. items.title: Social media users must be given copy of takedown order: Punjab and Haryana High Court
items.summary: The Punjab and Haryana High Court recently said that authorities ordering takedown of a social media page must also inform the user while notifying the intermediary [Haryana 24 News Network Private Limited v Union of India and Others] Justice Tribhuvan Dahiya made the observation while setting aside an order passed by the Haryana Police directing takedown of the Facebook page of Haryana 24 News Network Private Limited. The Court noted that Rule 3(2) of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 does not explicitly lay down the requirement to notify the user whose content or page is ordered to be taken down by the authorities. However, it observed that this requirement is an essential obligation ingrained in the principles of natural justice and has to be read into the rule. “Accordingly, a copy of the intimation must be furnished to the user when it is sent to the intermediary. This will make the procedure of sub-rule (2) to Rule 3 compliant of the primary tenets of natural justice and constitutionally valid,” the Court said. A Bench of Justices JB Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran passed the order while issuing extensive directions to detect and remove child sexual exploitation and abuse material (CSEAM) online. The Court said that internet access, as a fundamental right under Article 21 read with Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution, is available to children as well as adults. “We have no hesitation in saying that the right to access and use the internet is a fundamental right of every individual under Article 21 read with Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution. items.title: PIL in Calcutta High Court seeks double-side printing on A4 paper for pleadings in West Bengal courts
items.summary: A Public Interest Litigation (PIL) has been filed before the Calcutta High Court seeking a uniform mandate for filing physical pleadings and documents in 75 GSM A4 paper in duplex (back-to-back) format in the High Court and other courts across West Bengal [Akash Sharma v. Registrar General, High Court at Calcutta and Another] . The PIL aims to lower paper consumption, printing services and costs and the physical bulk of court records. The case is listed for hearing on November 23. Calcutta High Court on February 22, 2021 had asked its administrative side to consider mandating use of A4 paper with double-side printing for pleadings and filings. However, the plea filed by advocate Akash Sharma states that further progress of the matter could not be ascertained through publicly available records or notices. This PIL primarily seeks to determine the outcome of the order dated February 22, 2021 and a fresh consideration of the matter to prescribe a uniform practice of using 75 GSM A4 paper in a duplex-printed format across all courts in the State.
